doc.title: Rossano Sportiello interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, October 2, 2015 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Learning to do anything from Milan's TV orchestra musicians
summary: Older classically trained session players taught him versatility and how to fake a song and carry on after mistakes, as Rubinstein and Horowitz did.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: But there was, then in Milan, and some of them are still around, a group of musicians, for example, the musicians that worked for the orchestra of the TV, the national TV, that they had the kind of training that allowed them to do anything. I mean they were mostly classically trained musicians that loved jazz, so very early they learned to improvise and the jazz repertoire. But then of course growing up, some of them, even in the 40s and 50s that was when there was so much work for live music that every musician was supposed to be playing anything. So you were supposed to know waltzes and mazurkas and tangos but also the American songbook and to improvise, the bebop, everything. So by starting to play very early with these guys I understood how important it was to be able to pull it off in any situation you know. Or to turn any situation that you know that it might end up — it might be a stinky situation — you have to be able to turn it into a success. And these guys were unbelievable. I mean there were singers that, they knew anything. Anything that someone, “could you do that?” “Oh yeah, of course.” And then I learned very, very early, the importance of being able to fake a song. That sounds so bad, but it’s a big part of musicianship, you know, just if you’re not sure about something, you open your ears and you kind of fake it. You find your way through. And most of all you pretend like you know what you’re doing.
Very important. Yeah. This is what it’s supposed to be, whatever I’m playing.

Yes. Well you know that’s part of it. And you see that also in great concert artists you know. Those beautiful videos that you see now of Arthur Rubenstein and Vladimir Horowitz. Sometimes their playing is extraordinary. It’s out of this world. But they also made mistakes. They also — but you have to pretend like nothing happened. You cannot stop. You cannot make a face. You cannot make a face. You don’t do that. You just carry on. That’s very important.
